questions.stem: Physiological hyperplasia and hypertrophy are seen simultaneously in? Uterus in pregnancy Skeletal muscle in athletes Breast at puberty Left ventricle of heart in hypertensive patients
questions.solutionHtml:
w Roman",serif">Ans. C) Both 1 and 3

 

Explanation:

 

Option 1: During pregnancy, the uterus undergoes both hyperplasia (increased number of cells) and hypertrophy (increase in the size of existing cells) as a physiological response to accommodate and support the developing fetus. This dual increase in size and number of cells allows the uterus to significantly expand during pregnancy.

 

Option 2:  Athletes who undergo rigorous training often experience skeletal muscle hypertrophy, which is the increase in the size of muscle cells, but not typically hyperplasia, which would be an increase in the number of muscle cells. Muscle growth in athletes is usually attributed to hypertrophy from repetitive use and strain.

 

Option 3: During puberty, the female breast displays both hyperplasia, with the proliferation of glandular epithelium, and hypertrophy, with the enlargement of the glandular epithelial cells. This dual change is stimulated by hormonal influences and is a natural part of sexual maturation.

 

Option 4: In hypertensive patients, the left ventricle may undergo hypertrophy due to increased resistance that the heart has to pump against. This is not a physiological but rather a pathological response and typically does not involve hyperplasia, which would be characterized by an increased number of cardiac muscle cells.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In the uterus during pregnancy and the breast at puberty, physiological changes involve both hyperplasia (increase in the number of cells) and hypertrophy (increase in the size of cells). These changes are driven by hormonal influences that are part of natural growth and development processes.

tion:

Explanation:

It typically presents with a prolonged prothrombin time (PT) and activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT), which are not normal in this case.

 

Option C. von Willebrand disease: Von Willebrand disease is the most common hereditary bleeding disorder and is caused by a qualitative or quantitative deficiency of von Willebrand factor (vWF). vWF is crucial for platelet adhesion; however, PT and aPTT can be normal in mild cases, but there's often an abnormal bleeding time or abnormal vWF assays.

Similar to Glanzmann’s thrombasthenia, PT and aPTT are normal, but the platelet function is impaired, leading to bleeding.

questions.stem: A patient with Burkitt lymphoma presents with lethargy, weakness, and oliguria after receiving the first cycle of chemotherapy. Laboratory tests reveal abnormalities consistent with tumor lysis syndrome (TLS). Which of the following laboratory findings is LEAST likely to be associated with this condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
ysed cells.

 

Explanations

 

Option A. Hyperuricemia is typically seen in TLS due to the increased turnover of nucleic acids from rapid cell lysis, leading to excess production of uric acid.

 

Option B. Hyperkalemia results from the release of potassium, the most abundant intracellular cation, into the bloodstream when cells lyse.

 

Option C. Hyperphosphatemia occurs due to the release of intracellular phosphate into the extracellular fluid during cell lysis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Tumor lysis syndrome is characterized by hyperuricemia, hyperkalemia, and hyperphosphatemia, but not hypercalcemia; instead, hypocalcemia occurs due to the complexing of calcium with elevated phosphate levels.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman presents for evaluation of a hard, poorly defined mass in her left breast. She reports no pain or discharge, but she has noted a recent change in the shape of the breast. There is no family history of breast cancer. A mammogram reveals microcalcifications in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast. A biopsy of the lesion is performed. The type of mammary ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) most likely to result in a palpable abnormality in the breast is:
questions.solutionHtml:
:"Times New Roman",serif">Explanation:

 

Option A. Apocrine DCIS presents with characteristic apocrine cytologic features under microscopy but is not the most likely to form a palpable mass.

 

Option B. Neuroendocrine DCIS is a rare form and typically does not present as a palpable lesion in the breast.

 

Option C. Well-differentiated DCIS may show microcalcifications on mammography, but palpable masses are less common than in the comedo subtype.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Comedo DCIS is most likely to present as a palpable mass due to the associated necrosis and calcifications. It is often found on mammography and can form a more solid, palpable lesion compared to other subtypes of DCIS.

questions.stemHtml: A 35-year-old patient presents with unilateral sensorineural hearing loss and persistent tinnitus. Physical examination reveals a non-tender mass in the vicinity of cranial nerve VIII. An MRI indicates a well-circumscribed mass in the internal acoustic meatus, and a subsequent biopsy is performed. Histologically, the tissue demonstrates distinct regions of cellularity with areas showing dense proliferation of spindle cells, while others show less density. There is also evidence of nuclear palisading. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
ly:"Times New Roman",serif">Explanation:

 

Option B: Lymphoma: Lymphomas are neoplasms of the lymphatic system and would present histologically with an infiltration of lymphoid cells, which does not correspond to the nuclear palisading and alternating cellularity described in the stem.

 

Option C: Leukemia: This is a hematopoietic stem cell malignancy primarily affecting the bone marrow and blood. Histology of a solid mass would not reveal the characteristic findings of leukemia, such as blasts or excessive leukocytes.

 

Option D: Angiofibroma: Angiofibroma, often a benign tumor of adolescent males, would show a stromal and vascular component histologically, which is not described in the biopsy findings of the question stem.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The characteristic histological features of schwannomas are Antoni A areas, with hypercellular tissue and nuclear palisading, and Antoni B areas, which are less cellular.

questions.stem: Necrobiosis lipoidica is seen in:
questions.solutionHtml:
on:

 

Option A: Diabetes insipidus: This is a condition characterized by polyuria and polydipsia due to issues with vasopressin (ADH); it is not associated with skin changes like necrobiosis lipoidica.

 

Option B: Lyme disease: Caused by Borrelia burgdorferi and transmitted by ticks, Lyme disease can present with a variety of symptoms including erythema migrans, but not necrobiosis lipoidica.

 

Option D: Simmonds disease: Also known as Sheehan's syndrome, is postpartum hypopituitarism, not associated with necrobiosis lipoidica.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Necrobiosis lipoidica is a skin condition primarily associated with diabetes mellitus, presenting as well-circumscribed, waxy plaques typically on the shins with a yellowish center and telangiectatic borders.

Option D: Gall stones:  they can lead to obstructive jaundice, causing elevated levels of both conjugated and unconjugated bilirubin. However, the primary association is with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia.

Gilbert syndrome is a common inherited condition associated with unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia.

questions.stemHtml: A 24-year-old woman with a history of leukemia presents one month after a bone marrow transplant with a widespread scaling rash. She received a partially mismatched donor marrow. A skin biopsy is performed, and the histopathological findings show the presence of apoptotic cells. Which of the following biochemical reactions most likely explains these findings?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Activation of caspases

 

  • The histopathological findings in the skin biopsy, which show apoptotic cells, are indicative of graft-versus-host disease (GVHD).
  • In GVHD, donor immune cells attack the recipient's tissues, leading to apoptosis.
  • Apoptosis is mediated by a cascade of biochemical events involving the activation of caspases.
  • Caspases are proteolytic enzymes that play a crucial role in the execution phase of cell apoptosis, leading to the orderly and programmed dismantling of cellular components.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Reduction of ATP synthesis: This is typically associated with cellular necrosis rather than apoptosis. Necrosis results from severe ATP depletion and is characterized by cell swelling and rupture, not the orderly process seen in apoptosis.

 

Option B. Increase in glycolysis: While an increase in glycolysis can occur in various conditions, it is not specifically related to the apoptotic changes seen in this biopsy.

 

Option C. Activation of lipases: Lipase activation can occur in the context of cell injury leading to necrosis, particularly in the pancreas, but it is not directly related to the apoptotic process observed here.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The presence of apoptotic cells in a skin biopsy from a patient with a scaling rash after a bone marrow transplant is indicative of graft-versus-host disease, driven by the activation of caspases, leading to programmed cell death (apoptosis).

questions.stem: A 76-year-old man presents with a one-year history of abdominal pain. An abdominal CT scan shows a 10-cm mass in the pancreas. Biopsy reveals adenocarcinoma with inactivation of SMAD4. Which regulatory pathway is most likely altered?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) TGF-β

 

  • The inactivation of SMAD4 in pancreatic adenocarcinoma suggests an alteration in the TGF-β (transforming growth factor-beta) pathway.
  • SMAD4 is a key signal transducer in the TGF-β signaling pathway, which is involved in the regulation of cell growth, differentiation, and apoptosis.
  • Loss of SMAD4 function impairs TGF-β signaling, resulting in uncontrolled cell proliferation and tumor growth.

 

Other Options

 

Option A. BCL2: This gene is involved in regulating apoptosis by preventing cell death. It is not directly related to SMAD4 or the TGF-β pathway.

 

Option B. β-catenin: This protein is part of the Wnt signaling pathway and is involved in cell adhesion and transcription regulation. It is not associated with SMAD4 in the context described.

 

Option C. MYC: This oncogene regulates cell proliferation, growth, and apoptosis. While MYC can be altered in various cancers, it is not directly linked to the SMAD4 and TGF-β pathway.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Inactivation of SMAD4 in pancreatic adenocarcinoma disrupts the TGF-β signaling pathway, leading to diminished transcriptional activation of cyclin-dependent kinases and contributing to tumor growth.

questions.stem: A 53-year-old man presents with fatigue, weight loss, and splenomegaly. Laboratory tests reveal an elevated white blood cell count. Cytogenetic analysis shows the BCR-ABL fusion gene resulting from the t(9;22)(q34;q11) translocation. Which condition is most likely associated with this genetic finding?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Chronic myelogenous leukemia

 

  • The BCR-ABL fusion gene, resulting from the t(9;22)(q34;q11) translocation, is known as the Philadelphia chromosome and is characteristic of chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML).
  • This fusion gene encodes an abnormal tyrosine kinase that leads to uncontrolled cell proliferation, a hallmark of CML.

 

Other Options

 

Option A. Acute promyelocytic leukemia: This condition is associated with the t(15;17) translocation involving the PML-RARA gene, not BCR-ABL.

 

Option B. Follicular lymphoma: This is typically associated with the t(14;18) translocation involving the BCL2 gene, not BCR-ABL.

 

Option D. Hodgkin lymphoma, lymphocyte depletion type: This is not associated with the BCR-ABL fusion gene or the t(9;22) translocation.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The BCR-ABL fusion gene from the t(9;22) translocation is specifically associated with chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML), leading to uncontrolled proliferation of leukemic cells.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man has a 6-kg weight loss and nausea for the past 7 months without vomiting or diarrhea. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy reveals a 6-cm area of irregular, pale fundic mucosa and loss of rugal folds. Helicobacter pylori organisms are identified in mucus overlying adjacent mucosa. After antibiotic therapy for H. pylori, a repeat biopsy shows resolution of the infiltrate. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue tumor

 

  • The resolution of the lymphoid infiltrate after antibiotic therapy for Helicobacter pylori indicates a mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) tumor.
  • MALT lymphomas are often associated with chronic H. pylori infection, and eradication of the infection can lead to tumor regression.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Chronic gastritis: While chronic gastritis can be associated with H. pylori, it does not explain the lymphoid infiltrate and resolution after treatment.

 

Option B. Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma: This type of lymphoma would not typically resolve with antibiotic therapy for H. pylori.

 

Option C. Autoimmune gastritis: This condition is characterized by autoantibodies against parietal cells, not by H. pylori infection or lymphoid infiltrates.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) tumors are associated with H. pylori infection and can regress after eradication of the bacteria.

questions.stem: A 3-week-old neonate presents with increasing jaundice, hepatomegaly, and pale stools. A liver biopsy reveals marked proliferation of bile ducts, portal tract edema and fibrosis, and extensive intrahepatic and canalicular bile stasis. The infant's jaundice worsens progressively, and the infant dies of liver failure at 9 months of age. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Biliary atresia

 

  • Biliary atresia is a condition in which the bile ducts inside or outside the liver are abnormally narrow, blocked, or absent.
  • This leads to bile buildup in the liver, causing progressive liver damage.
  • The clinical presentation includes jaundice, hepatomegaly, and acholic (pale) stools.
  • The liver biopsy findings of bile duct proliferation, portal tract edema, fibrosis, and intrahepatic bile stasis are characteristic of biliary atresia.
  • If untreated, biliary atresia leads to worsening jaundice and liver failure.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Congenital toxoplasmosis: Presents with a range of symptoms including neurological deficits and chorioretinitis, but does not match the liver pathology described here.

 

Option B. α1-Antitrypsin deficiency: Can cause neonatal hepatitis and cholestasis but typically does not present with the severe bile duct proliferation and fibrosis seen in biliary atresia.

 

Option D. Choledochal cyst: Causes cystic dilatation of the bile ducts but is less likely to cause the described severe liver pathology and progression to liver failure seen in biliary atresia.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Biliary atresia is characterized by progressive jaundice, hepatomegaly, and acholic stools in neonates, with liver biopsy showing bile duct proliferation, fibrosis, and bile stasis, leading to liver failure if untreated.

questions.stemHtml: A biopsy was taken from the lymph node. What is name of the cell found in the lymph node? (FMGE JAN 2023)
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) RS cell

 

In the given image Reed-Sternberg cells are seen, which is seen in Hodgkin's lymphoma.

 

Reed-Sternberg cells marker -

  • CDI5
  • CD30 (most sensitive)
  • PAX-5 (most SPECIFIC)

 

RS cells are large and either multi-nucleated or have a bilobed nucleus which resemble as "owl's eye"

 

Reed-Sternberg (RS) cells are large, abnormal lymphocytes that are characteristic of Hodgkin's lymphoma (HL). There are four main types of HL, each with a different pattern of RS cell morphology.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Mott cell: These are plasma cells containing multiple globules of immunoglobulin and are not associated with Hodgkin's lymphoma.

 

Option C. Popcorn cell: This is a variant of RS cells seen in NLPHL, not the classic type shown in the image.

 

Option D. Plasma cell: These are antibody-producing cells derived from B-lymphocytes, not the characteristic cells in Hodgkin's lymphoma.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Reed-Sternberg (RS) cells, identifiable by their "owl's eye" appearance, are characteristic of Hodgkin's lymphoma and can be identified using markers like CD15, CD30, and PAX-5.

questions.stem: Which of the following feature associated with Barrett’s esophagus? (FMGE AUG 2020)
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Intestinal columnar metaplasia

 

Barrett's esophagus –

 

  • It is associated with GERD. The acid content of stomach comes upward to the lower part of esophagus. The esophagus is lined by squamous epithelium which is replaced by intestinal columnar epithelium
  • Squamous metaplasia – it is the commonest epithelial metaplasia which is associated with smoking. It affects the respiratory tract of smokers.

 

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Squamous Metaplasia: This type of metaplasia occurs when columnar epithelium is replaced by squamous epithelium. It is commonly seen in the respiratory tract of smokers.

 

Option C. Stratified Metaplasia: This term is not commonly used in the context of esophageal changes. Metaplasia usually refers to the transformation to a different type of epithelium rather than stratified epithelium.

 

Option D. Simple Columnar Metaplasia: This option refers to a type of metaplasia but does not specify the presence of goblet cells which are a hallmark of intestinal metaplasia in Barrett's esophagus.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Barrett’s esophagus is characterized by the replacement of the normal squamous epithelium of the esophagus with intestinal-type columnar epithelium, often as a result of chronic GERD.




ers to the transformation to a different type of epithelium rather than stratified epithelium.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old female suffered with heart disease and with cardiac atrophy. On H/E stain perinuclear, brown colored deposits were seen. Which pigment responsible for this? (FMGE DEC 2020)
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Lipofuscin

 

Lipofuscin: Injury of free radical, wear and tear pigmentation, also seen in cachexia, cancers. Lipofuscin is a Golden-brown pigment and called as pigment of aging. Sudan black B stain used.

 

 

 

Lipofuschin is also known as Wear & Tear pigment associated with aging, Perinuclear arrangements and Golden-brown color are characteristic of Lipofuscin.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Hemosiderin: This is an iron-storage complex found within cells, typically resulting from the breakdown of hemoglobin. It stains blue with Prussian blue stain (Pearl's reaction). Iron is usually stored in the form of Ferritin which then converts to Hemosiderin.

 

Option B. Stellate Cell: These are not pigments but specific cell types. In the liver, hepatic stellate cells are involved in fibrosis.

 

Option D. Calcium: Calcifications appear as dark purple or basophilic deposits on H&E staining, often indicating dystrophic or metastatic calcification.

 

Note - Melanin: black in color, identified with masson/ fontana stain.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Lipofuscin, identified by its golden-brown perinuclear deposits, is a marker of aging and cellular wear and tear, especially in long-lived cells like cardiac myocytes.

questions.stem: A Rh-ve mother had a pregnancy with a Rh+ve fetus. This Rh incompatibility is which of the following type of hypersensitivity reaction? (FMGE DEC 2021)
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Type II

 

Type II hypersensitivity reaction refers to an antibody-mediated immune reaction in which antibodies (IgG or IgM) are directed against cellular or extracellular matrix antigens, resulting in cellular destruction, functional loss, or damage to tissues. Damage can occur through multiple mechanisms.

 

 

Educational Objective

 

Rh incompatibility, where a Rh-negative mother produces antibodies against Rh-positive fetal red blood cells, is a Type II hypersensitivity reaction mediated by IgG or IgM antibodies.




ers to an antibody-mediated immune reaction in which antibodies (IgG or IgM) are directed against cellular or extracellular matrix antigens, resulting in cellular destruction, functional loss, or damage to tissues. Damage can occur through multiple mechanisms.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old female patient with a history of bee allergy came to the emergency room with complaints of swelling of face and dyspnea after a bee sting. Which of the following inflammatory mediators plays a major role? (FMGE JUNE 2021)
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Histamine

 

Inflammatory mediators, including cytokines, histamine, bradykinin, prostaglandins, and leukotrienes, impact the Immune system, usually as proinflammatory factors. Other mediators act as regulatory components to establish Homeostasis after injury or prevent the inflammatory process.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Serotonin: Also involved in the inflammatory response but not the primary mediator in allergic reactions like histamine.

 

Option B. Bradykinin: is a product of kallikrein induced breakdown of high-molecular-weight kininogen (HMWK) in the kinin cascade.

 

Option D. Prostaglandins: are a group of lipids with hormone-like actions that your body makes primarily at sites of tissue damage or infection.

 

Additional Information

 

 

Educational Objective:  

 

Histamine is the primary inflammatory mediator involved in the allergic response to a bee sting, leading to symptoms such as swelling and dyspnea.

questions.stem: Which one is most common macrocytic anemia in India? (FMGE JUNE 2022)
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Alcohol related

 

Chronic alcoholism is the most common cause of macrocytic anemia in India. The following mechanisms contribute to the development of macrocytic anemia in chronic alcoholics:

 

  1. Vitamin B12 deficiency: Alcohol interferes with the absorption and metabolism of vitamin B12, leading to deficiency.
  2. Folate deficiency: Alcohol consumption leads to poor dietary intake and absorption of folate, resulting in deficiency.
  3. Alcohol toxicity: Alcohol is directly toxic to the bone marrow, leading to abnormal erythropoiesis (the production of red blood cells).
  4. Megaloblastic anemia: Due to deficiencies in vitamin B12 and folate, which are essential for DNA synthesis in red blood cell production, resulting in the characteristic megaloblastic changes.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Sideroblastic anemia: A less common type of anemia caused by defects in heme synthesis, leading to the accumulation of iron in mitochondria.

 

Option B. Thalassemia: A genetic disorder resulting in abnormal hemoglobin production, more commonly associated with microcytic anemia rather than macrocytic anemia.

 

Option D. Chronic infection: Typically associated with anemia of chronic disease, which is usually normocytic or microcytic, not macrocytic.

 

Educational Objective

 

Chronic alcoholism

 

  1.  Vitamin B12 deficiency
  2. Folate deficiency
  3. Alcohol –toxic to marrow, abnormal erythropoiesis
  4. Megaloblastic anemia

questions.stem: Acid mucin is stained by _______? (AIIMS MAY 2018)
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Alcian blue

 

MUCIN STAINS:

 

  1. Alcian blue: Stains acid-simple non-sulfated and acid-simple mesenchymal mucins, acid-complex sulfated mucins and acid-complex connective tissue mucins. Does NOT stain neutral mucins
  2. Colloidal iron: Stains acid-simple non-sulfated, acid-simple mesenchymal, acid-complex sulfated mucins. Does NOT stain neutral mucins or acid-complex connective tissue mucins
  3. Mucicarmine: Very specific for epithelial mucins, including adenocarcinomas
  4. PAS (periodic acid-Schiff): Stains glycogen as well as mucins, but tissue can be pre-digested with diastase to remove glycogen. Stains neutral and acid-simple non-sulfated and acid-complex sulfated mucins. Does NOT stain acid-simple mesenchymal mucins and acid-complex connective tissue mucins

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. PAS: Stains both glycogen and mucins, but is not as specific as Alcian blue for acid mucins.

 

Option C. Masson trichrome: Primarily used for staining connective tissue (collagen) and is not specific for mucins.

 

Option D. PTAH (Phosphotungstic acid hematoxylin): Typically used for staining muscle striations, fibrin, and glial fibers, not for mucins.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Alcian blue is the preferred stain for identifying acid mucins in tissue samples, distinguishing it from other stains that target different types of mucins or tissue components.

questions.stem: A young boy from high altitude came with fever and weakness and had the following reports Hemoglobin 17 gm%, TLC is 21,000 with neutrophils 25, lymphocytes 30, eosinophils 5, myelocytes and metamyelocytes 40 in peripheral smear. Next step in the investigation should be: (AIIMS MAY 2019)

options.label: D
options.text: Bone Marrow biopsy with reticulin stain

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Erythropoietin levels

 

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of polycythemia (Hb>16 g/dL). Erythropoietin levels should be determined to differentiate primary from secondary forms.

 

Polycythemia vera (PCV) is characterized by increased marrow production of red cells, granulocytes, and platelets (panmyelosis), but it is the increase in red cells (polycythemia), that is responsible for most of the clinical symptoms. PCV must be differentiated from relative polycythemia resulting from hemoconcentration and other causes of absolute polycythemia. PCV is strongly associated with activating point mutations in the tyrosine kinase JAK2.

 

In PCV the progenitor cells have markedly decreased requirements for erythropoietin and other hematopoietic growth factors due to constitutive JAK2 signaling. Accordingly, serum erythropoietin levels in PCV are very low, whereas secondary forms of absolute polycythemia have high erythropoietin levels.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Philadelphia chromosome: This test is relevant in diagnosing chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), not polycythemia. While the presence of immature myeloid cells (myelocytes and metamyelocytes) could suggest a myeloproliferative disorder, the patient's clinical presentation and high hemoglobin level are more consistent with polycythemia, making erythropoietin testing a more appropriate next step.

 

Option B. JAK mutation: Testing for the JAK2 mutation is crucial in confirming a diagnosis of PCV. However, before proceeding to this test, it is important to measure erythropoietin levels to differentiate between primary and secondary polycythemia. If erythropoietin levels are low, JAK2 mutation analysis would then be the next step.

 

Option D. Bone Marrow biopsy with reticulin stain: This investigation is used to evaluate bone marrow fibrosis, which can occur in myeloproliferative disorders like PCV. However, it is not the first-line investigation in this scenario. The erythropoietin level is a less invasive test that provides critical information to guide further diagnostic steps.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Erythropoietin levels should be measured to differentiate between primary and secondary polycythemia. In cases of polycythemia vera, erythropoietin levels are typically low due to constitutive JAK2 signaling, while secondary polycythemia is associated with high erythropoietin levels.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old patient with a family history of endocrine tumors presents with recurrent episodes of peptic ulcers and diarrhea. Further evaluation reveals hypercalcemia and elevated levels of gastrin, insulin, and prolactin. Genetic testing confirms a mutation in the MEN1 gene. Which of the following best explains the mechanism underlying the patient's symptoms?

options.label: C
options.text: Loss of function of the menin protein

questions.answerText: Loss of function of the menin protein
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Loss of function of the menin protein

 

The patient presents with recurrent peptic ulcers, hypercalcemia, and elevated levels of gastrin, insulin, and prolactin, along with a family history of endocrine tumors. These findings are consistent with Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 1 (MEN1), also known as Wermer syndrome.

 

  • MEN1 is characterized by the 3Ps:
    1. Parathyroid hyperplasia or adenomas (leading to hypercalcemia).
    2. Pituitary tumors (e.g., prolactinomas causing elevated prolactin).
    3. Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (e.g., gastrinomas or insulinomas leading to peptic ulcers and hypoglycemia).
  • The MEN1 gene encodes menin, a tumor suppressor protein involved in regulating cell cycle and proliferation. Mutation of the MEN1 gene leads to loss of function of the menin protein, resulting in uncontrolled cell growth and tumor formation in multiple endocrine organs.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Overactivation of mTOR signaling: Overactivation of mTOR signaling is associated with tuberous sclerosis complex and certain sporadic cancers but is not the primary mechanism in MEN1.

 

Option B. Increased expression of RET proto-oncogene: The RET proto-oncogene is associated with MEN2 and MEN3 (now MEN2B). These syndromes involve medullary thyroid cancer, pheochromocytoma, and parathyroid hyperplasia or mucosal neuromas, but they do not involve pancreatic or pituitary tumors.

 

Option D. Dysregulation of PTEN tumor suppressor: PTEN dysregulation is associated with Cowden syndrome, which involves breast, thyroid, and endometrial cancers. It is not related to the endocrine neoplasms seen in MEN1.

 

Educational Objective:

 

MEN1 syndrome is caused by loss of function of the menin protein, leading to tumors in the parathyroid, pituitary, and pancreas. MEN1 is distinct from MEN2, which is associated with mutations in the RET proto-oncogene.

questions.stemHtml: A 50-year-old man presents with low grade fever, malaise and enlarged cervical and supraclavicular lymph nodes. The biopsy from one of the cervical nodes shows effaced architecture and sheet-like growth of small sized lymphocytes with irregular nuclear contours (as in image). Immunohistochemical analysis shows positivity for pan B cell markers, CD5 and cyclin D1. The diagnosis in this case is.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Mantle cell lymphoma

 

The provided histopathological image shows a monotonous proliferation of small lymphocytes with irregular nuclear contours, which is highly suggestive of mantle cell lymphoma (MCL). The immunophenotypic markers confirm the diagnosis:

 

  1. CD5 positivity – MCL is a CD5-positive B-cell lymphoma.
  2. Cyclin D1 positivity – A hallmark of MCL, resulting from t(11;14) translocation, leading to overexpression of cyclin D1, which promotes uncontrolled cell proliferation.
  3. Effaced lymph node architecture – A typical feature of aggressive lymphomas, including MCL.

 

MCL typically presents in middle-aged or older men with generalized lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, and bone marrow involvement. It is more aggressive than other small B-cell lymphomas, with a poor prognosis despite initial responsiveness to chemotherapy.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Follicular lymphoma:

 

  • Follicular lymphoma lacks CD5 and cyclin D1 expression.
  • It typically shows follicular growth patterns, unlike the sheet-like growth in this case.

 

Option B. Hairy cell leukemia:

 

  • Hairy cell leukemia is a CD5-negative B-cell neoplasm.
  • It is characterized by TRAP (tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase) positivity and a fried egg appearance of cells on histology, which is absent here.

 

Option D. Marginal zone lymphoma:

 

  • Marginal zone lymphoma is associated with chronic inflammation (e.g., H. pylori infection in gastric MALT lymphoma).
  • It is CD5-negative and cyclin D1-negative, making it unlikely in this case.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Mantle cell lymphoma is characterized by CD5 and cyclin D1 positivity, due to t(11;14) translocation.
  • It is more aggressive than other small B-cell lymphomas, with a poor prognosis.
  • Differential diagnosis includes follicular lymphoma (CD5-negative), hairy cell leukemia (CD5-negative, TRAP-positive), and marginal zone lymphoma (CD5-negative, associated with chronic inflammation).

questions.stemHtml: A 55-year-old female presents to the clinic with complaints of persistent swelling in her right arm following a radical mastectomy for breast cancer. The surgery was performed six months ago, and the patient has been undergoing adjuvant therapy since then. Physical examination reveals significant edema and thickening of the right arm, and the skin over the affected area appears erythematous and indurated. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the patient's arm swelling?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. Lymphedema

Postmastectomy edema (also known as postmastectomy lymphedema) is a common complication following radical mastectomy for breast cancer. It is characterized by persistent swelling in the arm on the side of the mastectomy, typically occurring several months to years after the surgery.   1. Cellulitis: Cellulitis can cause localized swelling, erythema, and induration of the skin.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old male undergoes a central venous catheter insertion for intravenous access during a surgical procedure. Shortly after the catheter insertion, the patient develops sudden-onset dyspnea, tachycardia, and hypotension. Physical examination reveals “mill-wheel” murmur over the precordium. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the patient's symptoms?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Air embolism 

 

Clinical Scenario Recap:

 

  • Procedure: Central venous catheter (CVC) insertion
  • Onset: Sudden
  • Symptoms: Dyspnea, tachycardia, hypotension
  • Exam Finding: “Mill-wheel” murmur — a classic hallmark

 

Why it’s Air Embolism:

 

  • Air embolism is a known complication of CVC insertion, especially when:
    • The patient is upright or hypovolemic
    • Proper technique is not followed (e.g., not occluding the catheter hub)
       
  • Pathophysiology: Air enters the venous circulation → reaches the right heart → causes obstruction to pulmonary blood flow.
     
  • Mill-wheel murmur = churning, splashing sound from air-blood interface in the right heart – highly characteristic.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Pulmonary embolism: Can cause similar symptoms but not typically associated with mill-wheel murmur or directly after CVC insertion.

 

Option C. Pneumothorax: May follow CVC insertion, especially via subclavian vein, but usually presents with unilateral decreased breath sounds, not a murmur.

 

Option D. Atelectasis: Can cause hypoxia, but not sudden hypotension or murmur; typically a gradual complication.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The presence of a mill-wheel murmur strongly points to air embolism, especially following central venous access procedures.
